items.prompt: After a successful login, where does the actual session data (e.g. which user this is) get stored?
choices: Inside the cookie itself, encoded as text
In a server-side record, referenced by an ID the cookie carries
In the URL of every request
Nowhere — the browser re-sends the password each time
items.explanation: A traditional session cookie carries only an opaque ID. The actual data — which user, what permissions — is stored server-side, indexed by that ID. The cookie is a pointer, not the payload.
items.reference:
Session

server-side record, indexed by a session ID

Cookie

just the ID, sent by the browser automatically

Why: the cookie is only a pointer — the actual session data lives on the server, not inside the cookie itself.

items.prompt: A teammate says 'the cookie contains the user's login info.' For a classic session-based login, is that accurate?
choices: Yes, cookies always contain the full user record
No — the cookie usually only carries a session ID; the record lives server-side
No — cookies can never carry any identifying data
Yes, but only for admin users
items.explanation: For session-based auth, the cookie is deliberately kept small and opaque — just an ID. The server looks that ID up in its own store to find the actual user record. (JWTs invert this, which L1's next section covers.)
items.reference:
Session

server-side record, indexed by a session ID

Cookie

just the ID, sent by the browser automatically

Why: the cookie is only a pointer — the actual session data lives on the server, not inside the cookie itself.

items.prompt: Which of these three fixes removes the need for any server to keep session data at all?
choices: Sticky sessions
A shared session store (e.g. Redis)
A stateless token (JWT)
None of them — some server-side storage is always required
items.explanation: A stateless token carries its own data in the request, so no server anywhere needs to store anything about the session. Sticky sessions and a shared store both still keep the data on a server — one on a single machine, one centralized.
items.reference:
Sticky

pins user to one server

Shared store

central store, extra hop

Stateless token

no server-side store

Why: only a stateless token removes the server-side dependency entirely — the other two just relocate it.

items.prompt: Which fix adds an extra network round trip to every single request, in exchange for working across any number of servers?
choices: Sticky sessions
A shared session store (e.g. Redis)
A stateless token (JWT)
All three, equally
items.explanation: A shared store fixes the multi-server problem, but every request now needs a lookup against that store — a real, per-request network cost that sticky sessions and JWTs don't have (sticky sessions have no lookup at all; JWTs verify locally with no network call).
items.reference:

Why: only a stateless token removes the server-side dependency entirely — the other two just relocate it.

items.prompt: A JWT looks like header.payload.signature. What does the middle part (payload) contain?
choices: The algorithm used to sign the token
The claims — user ID, expiry, and any app-specific data
The cryptographic proof of integrity
Nothing — it's reserved for future use
items.explanation: The payload holds the claims: sub (user), exp (expiry), and whatever else the app puts in at issue time. The header names the algorithm, and the signature is the tamper-proof.
items.reference:
Header

which algorithm signed it

Payload

the claims (sub, exp, ...)

Signature

proof it wasn't altered

Why: each of the three dot-separated parts has one job — mixing up 'payload' and 'signature' is the most common mistake.

items.prompt: Which part of a JWT tells a verifier which algorithm (e.g. HS256) was used to sign it?
choices: The payload
The signature
The header
None — the algorithm is never stored in the token
items.explanation: The header is a small JSON object naming the algorithm (and token type). L3 covers why blindly trusting this field from the token itself, instead of hardcoding the expected algorithm server-side, is a real vulnerability.
items.reference:
Header

which algorithm signed it

Payload

the claims (sub, exp, ...)

Signature

proof it wasn't altered

Why: each of the three dot-separated parts has one job — mixing up 'payload' and 'signature' is the most common mistake.

items.prompt: What is the signature part of a JWT actually proof of?
choices: That the payload is encrypted and unreadable
That the header and payload haven't been altered since signing
That the user's password was correct
That the token has not expired
items.explanation: The signature is a cryptographic proof of integrity: recomputing it from the received header+payload and comparing to the token's signature reveals whether either was changed after signing. It says nothing about encryption or expiry — those are separate concerns.
items.reference:

Payload

Signature

proof it wasn't altered

Why: each of the three dot-separated parts has one job — mixing up 'payload' and 'signature' is the most common mistake.

items.prompt: Can a user open their browser's dev tools, copy their own JWT, and read its payload claims in plain text?
choices: No, the payload is encrypted
Yes — the payload is only base64url-encoded, not encrypted
Only if they know the server's secret key
Only for expired tokens
items.explanation: JWTs are signed, not encrypted, by default. Base64url is a reversible encoding, not a cipher — anyone can decode a JWT's header and payload with nothing more than a text editor. The signature stops tampering, not reading.
items.reference:
Read

anyone can decode the payload

Tamper

signature blocks silent edits

Why: base64url is an encoding, not encryption — never put secrets you don't want the client to read inside a JWT payload.

items.prompt: A developer wants to put a user's plaintext password into a JWT payload 'because it's signed, so it's safe.' Is that reasoning sound?
choices: Yes — a signature makes any payload data confidential
No — signing proves integrity, not confidentiality; the payload is still plainly readable
Yes, but only if the token is short-lived
No — JWTs cannot hold any sensitive data under any circumstances
items.explanation: Signing guarantees the payload wasn't tampered with; it does nothing to hide it. Anything placed in a JWT payload should be treated as fully visible to whoever holds the token (and often to browser extensions, logs, or proxies), never as confidential.
items.reference:
Read

Tamper

signature blocks silent edits

Why: base64url is an encoding, not encryption — never put secrets you don't want the client to read inside a JWT payload.

items.prompt: After login, how does a session ID typically get from the server back to the browser?
choices: The server includes it in a Set-Cookie response header
The client has to manually poll a /session endpoint
It's embedded in every URL the user clicks
It's stored in the page's HTML as a hidden field
items.explanation: The server responds with a Set-Cookie header. The browser stores that value automatically and, from then on, attaches it as a Cookie header on requests that match the cookie's domain/path — no application code has to manage this resending.
items.reference:
Set-Cookie

server tells browser to store it

Cookie

browser auto-resends it later

Why: cookies are automatic on both ends — the server sets them once, and the browser resends them on every matching request without any app code asking it to.

items.prompt: Once a browser has stored a session cookie, does application JavaScript need to explicitly attach it to every fetch() call for the server to see it?
choices: Yes, always
No — the browser attaches matching cookies automatically
Only for POST requests
Only if the cookie is marked httpOnly
items.explanation: Cookie resending is a browser behavior, not something application code triggers — any request to a matching domain/path automatically carries the cookie. (This automatic-resend behavior is exactly what makes CSRF a concern for cookie-based auth, covered in L3.)
items.reference:

Why: cookies are automatic on both ends — the server sets them once, and the browser resends them on every matching request without any app code asking it to.

items.prompt: In a JWT payload, what does the exp claim represent?
choices: The user's experience level
A timestamp after which the token should no longer be trusted
The number of times the token has been used
The algorithm's expected output length
items.explanation: exp (expiry) is a Unix timestamp; a verifier should reject the token once the current time passes it. It's the main lever for limiting how long a stolen token stays useful.

sub

exp

Why: sub and exp are the two claims worth knowing by name — everything else in the payload is app-specific.

items.prompt: What does the sub claim conventionally identify in a JWT payload?
choices: The subject line of a notification email
The subject — i.e. which user or entity the token is about
The subscription tier of the account
The server that issued the token
items.explanation: sub is short for 'subject' — conventionally the user ID (or other principal) the token is asserting facts about. It's the claim a server reads first to know whose request this is.

items.prompt: A shared Redis session store lets every server recognize every user, same as a JWT would. Why is the Redis approach still called 'stateful'?
choices: Because Redis is slower than a JWT check
Because the session state still lives on a server-side system (Redis) that must stay available
Because Redis cannot be scaled horizontally
There's no real difference — both are equally stateless
items.explanation: Statelessness is about where the session data lives, not about how many servers can access it. A Redis-backed session still depends on a server-side store staying up and reachable; a JWT carries its data in the request itself, with no server-side store at all.
items.reference:
Redis-backed

state lives on a server (Redis)

JWT

state travels in the request

Why: statelessness is about where the state lives, not whether multiple servers can reach it — a shared store is still a server-side dependency.

items.prompt: Which property makes an authentication scheme genuinely 'stateless,' as opposed to merely 'shared across servers'?
choices: Any server can handle any request
No server anywhere has to store session data between requests
The session data is stored in a fast in-memory cache
Requests are encrypted end-to-end
items.explanation: 'Any server can handle any request' is true of both a shared store and a stateless token — it's necessary but not sufficient. The distinguishing property is whether any server-side store exists to depend on at all.
items.reference:
Redis-backed

state lives on a server (Redis)

JWT

state travels in the request

Why: statelessness is about where the state lives, not whether multiple servers can reach it — a shared store is still a server-side dependency.

items.prompt: An app uses sticky sessions and an aggressive autoscaler that removes servers every few minutes. Does sticky routing still protect a user's session from being lost?
choices: Yes, sticky sessions guarantee the session survives
No — once the pinned server is removed, that user's session is gone exactly as before
Yes, as long as the load balancer retries automatically
No — sticky sessions never worked in the first place, autoscaler or not
items.explanation: Sticky sessions only guarantee routing consistency while the pinned server exists. An autoscaler doesn't coordinate with sticky routing at all — when it removes that server, the in-memory session goes with it, and the user is logged out just like the original L1 scenario, only less frequently.
items.reference:
Autoscaler removes server

sticky routing has nothing left to pin to

Why: sticky sessions narrow the failure window (only lose the session when *your* server goes away) — they don't close it.

items.prompt: What's the most accurate way to describe what sticky sessions actually fix?
choices: They eliminate the multi-server session problem entirely
They reduce how often the problem occurs, but don't remove the underlying dependency on one server's memory
They move session storage to a database
They make every server aware of every other server's sessions
items.explanation: Sticky sessions keep routing consistent as long as the target server is alive, which reduces how often a user hits a server that doesn't know them — but the session is still only stored in that one server's memory, so any removal or restart of that server still loses it.
items.reference:
Autoscaler removes server

sticky routing has nothing left to pin to

Why: sticky sessions narrow the failure window (only lose the session when *your* server goes away) — they don't close it.

items.prompt: When a server verifies a JWT's signature, what is it actually doing?
choices: Looking up the token in a central database
Decrypting the payload with a private key
Recomputing the signature from the received header+payload and comparing it to the one in the token
Checking the token against a list of banned tokens
items.explanation: Verification recomputes the HMAC (or other algorithm) over the header and payload exactly as received, using the shared secret, and compares the result to the signature already in the token. A mismatch means the content was altered — or never signed by anyone holding the secret.
items.reference:
Recompute

server recomputes HMAC from received bytes

Compare

matches original signature?

Why: verification is pure computation against the shared secret — no network call, no shared store, which is exactly why it scales to any number of servers.

items.prompt: Why does JWT verification not require a network call to a database, unlike a shared-session-store lookup?
choices: Because JWTs are always small enough to cache
Because verification is pure computation against a secret the server already holds — nothing external needs to be consulted
Because JWTs are never checked on every request
Because the browser performs the verification, not the server
items.explanation: Signature verification only needs the token itself and the secret/key the verifying server already has locally. There's nothing to look up externally, which is exactly why it adds no network round trip and scales to any number of servers with zero shared infrastructure.
items.reference:
Recompute

server recomputes HMAC from received bytes

Compare

matches original signature?

Why: verification is pure computation against the shared secret — no network call, no shared store, which is exactly why it scales to any number of servers.

items.prompt: If the recomputed signature does not match the signature inside the token, what should the server conclude?
choices: The token is simply old and needs refreshing
The header or payload was altered after signing (or the token wasn't signed with the expected secret) — reject it
The user needs to clear their browser cache
The token is valid but for a different endpoint
items.explanation: A signature mismatch means the bytes being verified don't match what was originally signed — either they were tampered with, or the token was never legitimately signed with the secret the server expects. Either way, the correct response is outright rejection, not a partial trust.
items.reference:

Why: verification is pure computation against the shared secret — no network call, no shared store, which is exactly why it scales to any number of servers.

items.prompt: Who decides what values go into a JWT's claims (like role or tenantId)?
choices: The client, when it sends the request
The issuing server, at the moment it signs the token
Whoever holds the token, at any time
The load balancer, based on routing rules
items.explanation: Claims are set by the server at issue time (login), then locked in by the signature. The client can read them afterward but has no legitimate way to change them — any edit invalidates the signature, per L2's verification model.
items.reference:
Client

can read claims, cannot set them

Server

sets every claim at issue time

Why: the client only ever carries a token — it never gets a say in what the (already-signed) claims say.

items.prompt: A client sends a request with a JWT whose payload has been decoded, edited to add "role":"admin", and re-encoded — without re-signing. What happens on verification?
choices: The server accepts it since role is just data
The server rejects it — the recomputed signature won't match the edited payload
The server silently ignores the role claim
The server upgrades the user's role automatically
items.explanation: Any edit to the payload changes the bytes fed into signature recomputation. Without the secret to produce a matching signature for the new payload, verification fails and the token is rejected — this is the entire point of signing.
items.reference:
Client

can read claims, cannot set them

Server

sets every claim at issue time

Why: the client only ever carries a token — it never gets a say in what the (already-signed) claims say.

items.prompt: A support engineer needs to immediately force-logout a compromised account. Which is easier to do instantly: a shared-store session, or a bare JWT?
choices: A bare JWT — just discard it
A shared-store session — delete the record and the very next lookup fails
Both are equally instant
Neither can ever be revoked
items.explanation: A shared session store can delete the record immediately, so the next lookup fails right away. A bare JWT has no server-side record at all — there's nothing to delete, so it stays valid to any verifying server until its own exp claim passes.
items.reference:
Session

delete the record, instant logout

JWT

no record to delete, valid until exp

Why: a JWT has no server-side record to delete — 'revoke it' has nothing to act on until exp passes.

items.prompt: Why can't a JWT be revoked the same way a traditional session can?
choices: JWTs are encrypted so nobody can revoke them
There's no server-side record for a plain JWT — revocation has nothing to delete
JWTs never expire, unlike sessions
Revocation is a browser feature, not a server feature
items.explanation: Traditional session revocation works by deleting a server-side record. A plain JWT was never stored anywhere server-side to begin with, so there's no record to delete — the token remains verifiable (and therefore valid) until its own exp claim passes.
items.reference:
Session

delete the record, instant logout

JWT

no record to delete, valid until exp

Why: a JWT has no server-side record to delete — 'revoke it' has nothing to act on until exp passes.

items.prompt: What does verifying a JWT cost per request, compared to a shared-store lookup?
choices: Exactly the same — both need a network call
A local signature computation (CPU), with no network round trip
Nothing at all — verification is free
More than a shared-store lookup, since crypto is always slower than a query
items.explanation: JWT verification is a local cryptographic computation against a secret/key the server already holds — no network call required. It's not literally free (CPU time isn't zero), but it avoids the network round trip a shared-store lookup requires on every request.
items.reference:
Sticky

no cost, until it breaks

Shared store

network round trip per request

JWT

CPU signature check, no network

Why: the JWT approach trades a network round trip for a local CPU computation — much cheaper at scale, but not literally free.

items.prompt: Which statement best compares the per-request cost of the three approaches from L2's comparison table?
choices: Sticky sessions cost the most; JWTs cost the least
Sticky sessions have no per-request check at all; a shared store adds a network hop; a JWT adds a local CPU check
All three cost exactly the same per request
JWTs require two network calls per request, more than a shared store
items.explanation: Sticky sessions add no per-request lookup (the cost shows up later, as an outage when the pinned server disappears). A shared store adds a real network round trip per request. A JWT adds a local signature check — CPU cost, not network cost.

items.prompt: Implement base64urlEncode(str): encode a UTF-8 string to base64url text — url-safe characters, no trailing = padding. This is the encoding step every JWT header and payload goes through before being joined with dots.

tests.description: encodes a plain ASCII string
encodes a multi-byte UTF-8 string correctly
the empty string encodes to the empty string
output never contains standard base64's +, /, or = characters
tests.expr: expect(/[+/=]/.test(base64urlEncode("a string with enough bytes to need padding"))).toBe(false)

items.explanation: TextEncoder turns the string into its actual UTF-8 byte sequence (not just its UTF-16 code units), btoa base64-encodes those bytes, and the three .replace() calls make the result URL-safe: base64's + and / are swapped for - and _ (both legal in URLs and JWTs), and trailing = padding is stripped since JWTs never include it.
items.reference:
Encode

bytes -> url-safe text, no padding

Decode

url-safe text -> original bytes

Why: base64url swaps +/ for -_ and drops padding so the result is safe to put directly in a URL or a JWT, unlike plain base64.

items.prompt: Implement base64urlDecode(str): reverse base64urlEncode, turning url-safe text back into the original UTF-8 string. The tricky part: base64url strips padding, so you have to add it back before the browser's atob() will accept the string.

tests.description: decodes back to the original ASCII string
decodes back to the original multi-byte UTF-8 string
the empty string decodes to the empty string
round-trips through an encode/decode you'd also need to trust

items.explanation: The url-safe substitutions are undone first (- back to +, _ back to /), then padding is restored — atob() requires the input length to be a multiple of 4, and "===".slice((len+3)%4) computes exactly how many = characters were stripped off. atob() gives back a binary string; wrapping each character code in a Uint8Array and running it through TextDecoder correctly reassembles multi-byte UTF-8 characters instead of mangling them.
items.reference:
Encode

bytes -> url-safe text, no padding

Decode

url-safe text -> original bytes

Why: base64url swaps +/ for -_ and drops padding so the result is safe to put directly in a URL or a JWT, unlike plain base64.

items.prompt: This base64urlEncode has a bug — it produces output that isn't actually safe to embed in a URL or JWT. Find and fix it.

tests.description: output never contains +, /, or =

tests.description: still encodes correctly
empty string still encodes to empty string

items.explanation: The original returned raw btoa() output — standard base64, which can contain +, /, and trailing = characters. All three are meaningful in a URL (+ can mean a space, / is a path separator, = is often a query-parameter delimiter) or awkward inside a dot-separated JWT, so a real base64url implementation must substitute them and drop padding before the value is safe to use as a URL or token segment.

items.prompt: Implement isWellFormedJwt(token): return true only if the token has exactly 3 dot-separated, non-empty segments (header, payload, signature). This is the first check a review should look for before any decoding happens.

tests.description: a normal 3-part token is well-formed
a token missing the signature part is not well-formed
a token with an empty payload segment is not well-formed
a token with an extra segment is not well-formed

items.explanation: Splitting on "." and checking the resulting array has exactly 3 non-empty entries catches every structurally invalid shape — too few parts, too many parts, or an empty segment (like two dots in a row) — in one check, before any base64url decoding or JSON parsing is attempted on data that might not even be well-formed enough to decode.

header.payload.signature

Anything else

malformed — reject before reading claims

Why: a token with the wrong number of dot-separated parts should never reach claims logic at all — reject it at the structural check, before any decoding is attempted.

throws on a 2-part token instead of returning undefined

items.prompt: This structural check has a subtle bug: it uses String.prototype.split with a limit argument, which silently truncates instead of detecting extra segments. Find and fix it so a 4-part token is correctly rejected.

tests.description: a normal 3-part token is still well-formed
a token with an extra 4th segment is correctly rejected
a 2-part token is still rejected

items.explanation: JavaScript's split(separator, limit) stops collecting once it reaches limit results and silently drops everything after — it does not verify there was nothing left over. "aa.bb.cc.dd".split(".", 3) returns ["aa","bb","cc"], the same as a genuinely well-formed token, so the extra segment goes completely undetected. Splitting with no limit and checking the full resulting length is the only way to actually catch it.

items.prompt: Implement isExpired(payload, nowSeconds): return true if the payload's exp claim exists and nowSeconds has reached or passed it. A payload with no exp claim should never be considered expired by this function.

tests.description: not yet expired one second before exp
expired at the exact exp timestamp
expired well after exp
a payload with no exp claim is never considered expired

items.explanation: exp is defined by the JWT spec as Unix seconds, so the comparison only makes sense if the caller also passes seconds — mixing this up with Date.now() (milliseconds) is a classic bug that makes tokens look expired ~1000x too early, or not expired at all. Using >= (not >) treats the exact expiry second as already expired, matching how most real JWT libraries behave.
items.reference:
exp

seconds since epoch, not ms

now >= exp

expired, reject

Why: exp is always Unix seconds — comparing it against Date.now() (milliseconds) without converting is a real, common off-by-1000x bug.

items.explanation: A signed remaining-time value (rather than a boolean) is what a client actually needs to decide when to refresh a token ahead of expiry, not just after the fact. Infinity for a missing exp claim keeps the return type numeric and comparable (e.g. "refresh if less than 60 seconds left") without needing a special undefined case at every call site.

items.prompt: This expiry check has the classic units bug: it compares a Unix-seconds exp claim against Date.now(), which returns milliseconds. Find and fix it.

tests.description: a token expiring far in the future is not expired right now
tests.expr: const future = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 3600; expect(isExpired({ exp: future }, Date.now())).toBe(false)

tests.description: a token that expired in the past is correctly expired
tests.expr: const past = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 3600; expect(isExpired({ exp: past }, Date.now())).toBe(true)

tests.description: a payload with no exp claim is never expired

items.explanation: Date.now() returns milliseconds since epoch; exp is always Unix seconds per the JWT spec. Comparing them directly makes now roughly 1000x larger than it should be, so any token with an exp less than about 50 years from now would look expired immediately — the fix converts now to seconds (Math.floor(now / 1000)) before comparing, matching the units exp is actually in.

items.explanation: Base64(url) encodes every 3 raw bytes as 4 encoded characters, so the encoded size is always about 4/3 of the raw size — this is exactly the growth curve the interactive demo above plots. The fixed overhead (header, base fields like sub/iat/exp, and the signature) exists even at zero extra claims, which is why estimateTokenSizeBytes(0) is still 133 bytes, not 0.

items.explanation: Walking numClaims up one at a time and stopping as soon as the next claim would exceed the budget finds the largest value that still fits, without needing to invert the rounding in estimateTokenSizeBytes algebraically — the loop naturally floors at 0 for a budget too small to hold even the fixed overhead, since the while condition simply never becomes true.

A capacity check or a 'will this fit in a cookie/header limit' calculation built on the unfixed version would systematically pass tokens that are actually too large once encoded.
